article.headline: The Resale Market Turning Canceled Vacations Into Bargains
article.lede: When a nonrefundable trip falls through, the money is usually gone with it. A small but growing category of online marketplace — think eBay for holidays — now lets sellers recover part of that loss while buyers travel at a discount. The model is straightforward; the risks are subtler.
article.body:
The mechanics are simple enough. Platforms like **SpareFare** (founded 2016), Roomer, Plans Change, and Transfer Travel let sellers list flights, hotel reservations, and package holidays they can no longer use. Buyers take over the reservation at a negotiated markdown. To limit fraud, the platforms hold payment in *escrow*, releasing funds to the seller only after the buyer has completed the trip. SpareFare charges a 12% commission per transaction.

Typical discounts run 20–30% off the original price. Buyers willing to wait until the 48 hours before departure can find steeper cuts, since last-minute sellers are focused on recovering whatever they can rather than maximizing the sale price. Retirees and remote workers — the most schedule-flexible cohort — make up the bulk of SpareFare's repeat buyers. The platform's largest single sale to date: a two-week Fiji trip originally priced at $46,000, picked up by a California investment manager for $33,000.

At the upper end of the market sits **Eluxit**, founded in 2019 by Bahar Schmidt, a Los Angeles travel agent, after a client had to abandon a $150,000 private charter to the Galápagos Islands at the last minute. Unlike SpareFare — which requires the seller to coordinate name changes directly with carriers and hotels — Eluxit handles that administrative work itself. Among its clients: Judy Schroffel, longtime executive assistant to California billionaire Anthony Pritzker, who used Eluxit to offload a Mexican villa booked around a concert he could no longer attend; it sold for fifty cents on the dollar. Schmidt operates within the *Internova* consortium, a luxury travel network of more than 100,000 agents she hopes to turn into a distribution channel for high-end unsold inventory.

The concept predates the internet. Henry Harteveldt, president of the travel consultancy Atmosphere Research, traces a cottage industry in resold travel to newspaper classifieds in the 1980s. Tighter identification requirements introduced after the September 2001 attacks made casual ticket transfers harder. Today the chief friction point is airline name-change policy, which varies by carrier and carries a hidden risk: software designed to flag money laundering and human trafficking may trigger on a last-minute name change, even an innocent one. Harteveldt recommends calling the airline before purchasing any secondhand flight.

concepts.definition: A travel reservation — flight, hotel night, or package — whose purchase price cannot be returned if the buyer cancels. Airlines and hotels typically price these fares lower upfront in exchange for keeping the money if plans change. The arrangement creates stranded value when genuine emergencies force cancellations, which resale platforms now try to recover.

An arrangement in which a neutral third party holds funds until a specified condition is met. In travel resale, the platform holds the buyer's payment until after the trip has occurred, reducing the risk that a seller collects money for a booking they no longer control or that was never real.

Rules set by individual carriers governing whether, and at what cost, a ticket may be reissued under a different passenger's name. Policies vary widely — many low-cost carriers prohibit changes entirely. A name-change request made close to departure can trigger automated compliance alerts originally designed to catch money laundering or human trafficking.

article.fact_check: The article's opening anecdote — Samina Ahmed paying roughly $1,200 for a Thailand trip originally priced at $4,700 — implies a discount of about 75%, far above the 20–30% range the same piece describes as typical. The article notes that last-minute deals run deeper, which may account for the gap, but leading with such an outlier risks giving readers an inflated sense of routine savings.
